name: Sam Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m a researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential. What is a normal shift like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Sam Torres, 58, and I drive a continuous miner at a large underground mine. I check the cutting head and ventilation reading, then work the face with the rest of the crew close by. The wage is good for this job, and I value the crew, but a bad air reading can spoil your whole morning.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who do you go home to?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Luis cooks most evenings, and our daughter is grown and works in another town. We have nearly a year of expenses saved and have kept the house payments current. There are several mines within a reasonable drive, but I would rather finish my working years with people who know each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the crew that a faster office form is fine if it does not replace the safety check at the face. I do not use AI tools, and I am not itching to start. The ventilation reading belongs in a real person’s hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be comfortable keeping my present shift and pay. Luis and I have almost a year of expenses saved, and my higher mine wage still lets us build toward retirement. I would worry more about a blocked ventilation line than a new form.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep checking the cutting head and air reading before starting each shift. I’d continue the standing transfer into our savings account each month. In the first year after the form changes, I’d tell the safety representative if a digital record misses a reading.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel calm, maybe relieved that the argument has shrunk to paperwork. I like knowing what work is mine. A steady roster would let Luis and me make ordinary retirement plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What kind of missing reading have you seen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last spring a tablet entry showed a blank where the air reading should have been. I pointed it out to the safety representative before we went back to the face, and I would do it again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much goes into savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We transfer two hundred each month after the house payment clears. Our daughter pays her own way, so that money is for our later years rather than school fees.

say: I’d accept **faster forms** while keeping a human ventilation check.
I would not swap the **air reading** for an office shortcut.
think: My **shift and pay** look secure in this mild picture.
Nearly a year of savings supports our **retirement plan**.
do: Check the **cutting head** and air reading each shift.
Transfer **two hundred monthly** to savings after the house payment.
Report a missing **digital reading** to the safety representative.
feel: **Calm** about steady work and ordinary retirement planning.
S0.quote: The ventilation reading belongs in a real person’s hands.
fieldNote: Sam’s concern stays on **mine safety**, especially complete air readings, rather than on modest office automation.
His **higher wage** and nearly yearlong cushion allow a regular transfer toward retirement without relying on his grown daughter.

steps.text: Keep operating the continuous miner after cutting-head and air checks
Transfer two hundred monthly into savings after the house payment

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say the booking and buying desks will change before a robot reaches our coal face. I would want the crew’s safety representative in the room when a new schedule is drawn. An algorithm can shorten a shift on paper and still leave someone breathing bad air.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I do not expect my own driving hours to disappear soon, with several mines nearby if this one cuts back. I worry that office staff will be dropped and the remaining workers rushed. Luis thinks I should learn the new system, but I would rather see evidence that it is safe first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d attend the next safety committee meeting and bring the old and new shift schedules to compare ventilation time. I’d keep driving the continuous miner under the current checks. During the first year I’d sign the crew petition for human review of any machine-made safety schedule.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel uneasy for coworkers and impatient with promises about efficiency. My wage still looks solid. I would be more settled if management sat with the people who work at the face.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the petition ask for exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would ask for a named safety officer to sign each changed ventilation schedule before it reaches the shift. I would sign that request with the crew, even if it slows the rollout.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move to another mine now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, there is work here and a move would break a crew I trust. Nearby mines are an option if a real cut happens, not a reason to leave this week.

say: I’d say **desk tasks** change before robots can cut rock at our underground face.
I’d demand **human review** of machine-made safety schedules.
think: My **driving hours** look stable, with nearby mines as an option.
Fewer office staff could mean **rushed crews** underground.
do: Compare **ventilation schedules** at the safety committee.
Keep driving the **continuous miner** under current checks.
Sign the crew **safety petition** during the first year.
feel: **Uneasy** for coworkers, while expecting my own wage to hold.
S1.quote: An algorithm can shorten a shift on paper and still leave someone breathing bad air.
fieldNote: Sam uses the **safety committee** to challenge scheduling changes, anchored in ventilation time rather than a general dislike of AI.
He expects **continued mine pay** and sees multiple nearby mines as a fallback if hours are cut.

steps.text: Keep driving the continuous miner under existing air checks
Sign the crew petition for human review of safety schedules

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the crew that full thinking AI in 2028 may erase many office posts, and machines able to cut rock like us arrive around 2031. I would push for a crew agreement on notice and severance before the machines are ordered. Nobody should have to learn they lost a shift from an app.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 60 at the AI date and 63 when capable robots could replace my work at the face. We have nearly a year saved and other mines nearby, but those mines may buy robots too. Losing my higher pay several years before I planned to stop would change our retirement figures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask our union branch to call a meeting this month and join a crew delegation seeking written notice and severance terms. I’d also request my retirement statement and check posted vacancies at the other mines. In 2029 I’d continue paid shifts if offered, and I’d apply for an advertised operator role elsewhere if this mine gives a firm cut date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel anxious about losing earnings, but I would not be frozen. Our savings buy time to look, not a replacement wage for all the years ahead. I would tell Luis the numbers as soon as we have them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn a robot control system?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would listen if the mine offered a paid course and a real post, but I would not spend our savings on a vague promise. A robot that can do the whole job may need few operators.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the delegation ask for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would ask for a notice period, severance amounts and access to actual open posts in writing. I would go with two crew members so the request is on the record.

say: I’d push for written **notice and severance** before robots are ordered.
I’d say **2028 office AI** precedes mine robots around 2031.
think: At **63**, I could lose higher pay years before planned retirement.
Nearby mines may also buy **robots**, despite our strong savings cushion.
do: Join a crew **delegation** for written notice and severance terms.
Request a **retirement statement** and check nearby vacancies.
Work paid shifts in **2029** and apply elsewhere after a firm cut date.
feel: **Anxious** about lost earnings, with savings and job options giving room to act.
S2.quote: Our savings buy time to look, not a replacement wage for all the years ahead.
fieldNote: Sam’s nearly yearlong **cushion** softens the first shock, but robot adoption across nearby mines could end expected higher wages.
He responds through a **crew delegation** and concrete applications, keeping paid shifts while they are available.

steps.text: Join the crew delegation seeking written notice and severance terms
Apply for an advertised nearby operator role after a firm cut date
Keep paid continuous-miner shifts through 2029 if offered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say the five-year warning gives us time to bargain over the change while crews are still needed. Thinking AI arrives in 2031, and cutting robots follow around 2034 when I would be 66. I would not accept a last-minute retirement offer without seeing its terms next to our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could be ready to stop at 66, given our savings, but I have not confirmed any pension amount. Luis has his own income from freelance painting, which varies by season. A few more good mine years would make it easier for both of us to slow down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the retirement provider for a written projection and put it beside our house payments with Luis. I’d keep the continuous-miner shifts while the mine still needs me. In 2032 I’d attend the union’s contract meeting and vote on a proposal for advance notice before any robotic cutover.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel uneasy but far less pressed than in the two-year picture. We could check the figures, see the agreement and choose when to leave if the offer is decent. I would not celebrate until the paperwork exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the projection comes back low?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep working mine shifts while available and look at one of the other local mines if ours cuts early. Luis and I would trim the travel budget before asking our daughter for help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does a union agreement guarantee your job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. It can make the timing and payment fairer, which is still worth the meeting and the vote. The actual wage depends on whether a shift remains.

say: I’d use the **five-year warning** to bargain while crews still work.
I’d insist on written **retirement terms** before accepting an exit.
think: At **66**, retirement may be affordable, but I need the pension figure.
Luis’s **painting income** varies, so mine wages still help.
do: Request a written **retirement projection** and list house payments.
Keep paid **miner shifts** while they exist.
Attend and vote at the **2032 contract meeting**.
feel: **Uneasy** about the terms, with time to calculate and bargain.
S3.quote: The actual wage depends on whether a shift remains.
fieldNote: Sam’s savings may support retirement near the **2034 robot date**, yet he wants a verified pension amount and house budget.
He sees a **union agreement** as a way to improve notice and payments, without mistaking it for guaranteed work.

steps.text: Keep paid continuous-miner shifts while available
Attend the 2032 union contract meeting and vote on notice terms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the crew a decade is enough time to make the retirement plan real and put safety lessons in writing. Thinking AI arrives in 2036, when I would be 68; capable cutting robots follow around 2039, when I would be 71. I do not expect to be at the face at 71.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I hope to stop mine work before the thinking AI date, but I will only promise that after Luis and I check the income figures. Our house payments will be lower by then if we stay on schedule. The robots may reshape the mine after I leave, but I still care about the younger crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d review our retirement account with Luis each winter and keep the current savings transfer while I earn. I’d stay on paid shifts until our agreed retirement date and write down the ventilation checks for the next operator. In 2037, if I have already retired, I’d take those notes to the safety representative and ask the union to keep the checks in the training book.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel calm about my own earnings over the next few years and concerned for the people following me. A decade gives me room to finish on our terms. I would still speak up about air checks after I put my helmet away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would go in the training book?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The sequence for checking the face air before the cutting head starts, including who to call when a reading is missing. I’d write it with the safety representative so it is usable on a real shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move your savings into new machines?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, Luis and I have savings for retirement, not capital to buy mine equipment. We would keep our own account and check its balance each year.

say: I’d make the **retirement plan** concrete over the decade.
I’d keep **air checks** in training after I leave.
think: I expect to leave the **mine face** before robots arrive around 2039.
I still need verified **income figures** before naming my final shift.
do: Review **retirement savings** with Luis each winter.
Keep paid shifts until our agreed **retirement date**.
Give **ventilation notes** to the safety representative in 2037 if retired.
feel: **Calm** about my own wages, with concern for younger crew members.
S4.quote: I would still speak up about air checks after I put my helmet away.
fieldNote: Sam expects **2039 robots** after his likely working years, while verifying income before fixing a retirement date.
He plans to preserve **ventilation checks** through written training notes and the safety representative, even after leaving paid mine work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 picture worries me most because the robots could end my higher mine wage at 63, before Luis and I planned to live off savings. Written notice, severance, a real vacancy list and an honest retirement statement would help. The crew should have a say while we still have work to bargain over.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what happens to safety when the person making the schedule has never breathed the mine air. I want the next crew to have a named safety officer and time to check the face. A clever plan on a screen does not move oxygen underground.

headlineQuote: A clever plan on a screen does not move oxygen underground.
portrait: Sam, **58**, drives a continuous miner and checks face ventilation with his crew.
His **higher pay** and nearly yearlong savings cushion give him choices, though he still counts on more earning years.
He avoids **AI tools** and pushes for safety review through crew and union action.
Fast robots could cut expected wages; a **decade** likely puts automation after his retirement.
biggestWorry: The **2028 picture** worries Sam most because cutting robots around 2031 could end his higher wages at 63.
whatWouldHelp: Written **notice**, severance, real vacancies and verified retirement figures would let him plan with Luis.
